clue.text: Only headgear of Top People allowed in the house

parts.note: a cap is a piece of headgear
U is the old label for upper-class usage, the speech of top people
to let is to allow or permit

explanation.surface: A dress code in some grand house where only the elite's hats are permitted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Only' and 'in the' are link words; the house is the family of Juliet in Romeo and Juliet, rivals of the Montagues.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's Verona the Capulets are one of the two feuding noble families, a house in the dynastic sense.

parts.note: in Martin Chuzzlewit Pecksniff's daughters are Mercy and her elder sister, also named for a virtue

explanation.surface: A nun from a Dickens novel.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'Sister of Mercy' looks like a nun, but Mercy is a Pecksniff girl whose sister bears a virtue's name too.
explanation.definitionFit: Charity Pecksniff is Mercy's sister in Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit, and charity sits beside mercy among the virtues.

indicators.note: the word for survive is placed inside the word for jetties

parts.note: piers are jetties running out into the water
to last is to survive or endure

explanation.surface: Pillars that hold up through time in harbour structures.
explanation.definitionFit: Pilasters are flat rectangular columns set into a wall.

parts.note: read as the parts that make up a chain rather than the smiths who forge one

explanation.surface: The people who forge chains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chain-makers' suggests blacksmiths, but it is the rings that together make a chain.
explanation.definitionFit: Each interlocking ring of a chain is one of the pieces that together form it.

parts.note: plays on the saying two's company, three's none, applied to a game for three players

explanation.surface: A game with no companions.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'two's company, three's none' makes any game for three people 'no company'.
explanation.definitionFit: A game played by three people, as in golf, is named for its three players.

parts.note: the winning side is on top
a side is a team in sport

explanation.surface: The victorious team turn out to be a hefty lot.
explanation.walkthrough: Topside is a British butcher's cut, a lean joint from the top of the hind leg of beef, hence 'decidedly beefy'.
explanation.definitionFit: Topside is a cut of beef, so nothing could be more thoroughly of the cow.

parts.note: Fido is Latin for I have faith, so telling a dog of that name to have faith is unnecessary

explanation.surface: A pointless command given to a dog.
explanation.walkthrough: Fido, the stock dog's name, is Latin for 'I trust' or 'I am faithful'.
explanation.definitionFit: Telling a dog called Fido, which in Latin already means I have faith, to have faith is a needless order.

parts.note: a base read as the foot of a statue rather than a low moral character

explanation.surface: A complaint that some fans are a low crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A base lot' sounds like contempt for a group of fans, but the supporters are the stands under statues.
explanation.definitionFit: Plinths that hold up statues or columns are bases that support them.

parts.note: split as a word meaning cross, i.e. angry, not a crossword puzzle

explanation.surface: A question about the crossword itself.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'crossword' split in two: a word that means cross.
explanation.definitionFit: An angry person is cross, and this is a word for that temper.

clue.text: Express approbation but it might mean the last straw for the camel

definitions.text: it might mean the last straw for the camel

explanation.surface: Giving approval that could prove one burden too many.
explanation.walkthrough: Latin dorsum is the back; the word literally means to put on the back, where the last straw broke the camel's.
explanation.definitionFit: To back or approve something publicly; literally to load onto the back, as the proverbial straw was.

clue.text: Exhausted by no holds being barred?

explanation.surface: Worn out by a no-holds-barred struggle.
explanation.walkthrough: All-in wrestling is the free style in which no holds are barred.
explanation.definitionFit: Being worn out means being utterly tired; all-in wrestling is the style in which every grip is permitted.

clue.text: But even a square could write in this manner

definitions.text: But even a square could write in this manner

parts.words: But even a square could write in this manner
parts.note: a style of penmanship named for a shape, so the joke is that a square person could still write with curves

explanation.surface: Even the most conventional person could manage this script.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'square' is a dull conventional person, set against the name of a bold, rounded style of handwriting.
explanation.definitionFit: Roundhand is a clear style of penmanship with full, curved letters, used by clerks and copyists.

indicators.note: the letters of the first words are offered in exchange for the answer, a rearrangement standing in for it

parts.note: taken as its letters ITS, with the apostrophe dropped
taken as written

explanation.surface: Tennis is the game for those who never give up.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal is only the word 'for': ITSTENNIS is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A persevering person keeps on pressing, refusing to let a demand drop.

explanation.surface: Some vehicle or animal that is awkward to handle.
explanation.walkthrough: One word is both a young castrated ox and the verb for guiding a vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: A bullock raised for beef is a farm beast; to guide a car or boat is to drive it.

explanation.surface: A complaint that surrender is a hackneyed move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corny' is read literally, as to do with corn: a farm's harvest of grain is its output.
explanation.definitionFit: A crop's output of grain is the harvest amount; to surrender or concede is to give up.

clue.text: Over-door feature that simply oozes class?

definitions.text: Over-door feature that simply oozes class?

parts.words: Over-door feature that simply oozes class?
parts.note: an architectural moulding above a door, read literally as stone that lets rain drip off

explanation.surface: A stylish feature above the front door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oozes class' is the cliché for stylish, but here it means literally oozing water.
explanation.definitionFit: A projecting moulding over a door or window throws off rain; it is also a name for limestone formed by dripping water.

clue.text: Send off with a show of shards

definitions.text: Send off with a show of shards

parts.words: Send off with a show of shards
parts.note: ancient Athenians voted to banish a citizen by scratching his name on pieces of broken pottery

explanation.surface: A dismissal accompanied by a display of broken pottery.
explanation.walkthrough: The word comes from Greek ostrakon, a potsherd used as a ballot in Athenian votes of exile.
explanation.definitionFit: To exclude someone from society comes from the Athenian vote of exile cast on potsherds.

clue.text: Call Buttons to open the book

parts.note: to title something is to name or call it
a page boy in a hotel was nicknamed Buttons for his uniform

explanation.surface: Summoning the bellboy to come and open the ledger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buttons' is the old British name for a uniformed page boy, as in pantomime.
explanation.definitionFit: The leaf at the front of a book bearing its name is the first thing seen on opening it.

clue.text: Nude tiler has a short break

indicators.note: the two words are held together as one pool of letters to be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A naked roofer stops for a quick rest.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no strong anagram signal; NUDE TILER is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A brief pause or intermission between parts of something is a short break.

indicators.note: the words are to be put differently, expressed in another arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as its letters LETS, the apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A clumsy remark followed by an exasperated attempt to phrase it better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put it' tells you to rephrase INEPT plus LETS, an anagram giving the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Plaguy is an old word for annoying or troublesome, like something carrying disease or a nuisance.

clue.text: "Each throat Was and glazed each eye" (Coleridge)

definitions.text: "Each throat Was and glazed each eye" (Coleridge)

parts.words: "Each throat Was and glazed each eye" (Coleridge)
parts.note: the missing word from the Ancient Mariner's account of the becalmed crew dying of thirst

explanation.surface: A line from The Rime of the Ancient Mariner with a gap.
explanation.walkthrough: The line runs 'Each throat / Was parched, and glazed each eye', the sailors becalmed without water.
explanation.definitionFit: A throat dried out by thirst is badly dry.

clue.text: Well, this physique has gained a lead at tennis

definitions.text: has gained a lead at tennis

explanation.surface: Commentary on a well-built player who has gone ahead in a tennis match.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'well set-up' person has a fine build; a tennis player who is a set ahead is said here to be 'set up'.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's build or frame is their physical arrangement; being a set ahead in tennis is having a lead.

clue.text: Bobbies in force up the street for drinks

parts.note: a posse is a body of police officers out in force; bobbies are British police

indicators.note: in a down clue the abbreviation is read upwards, from the bottom

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: Police arriving in numbers along the road to fetch a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns ST into TS. A posset is a hot drink of milk curdled with ale or wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Possets are old hot milky drinks curdled with wine or ale.

clue.text: Birds that are loud in the old country

indicators.note: the letters for loud are placed inside the letters for the country

parts.note: RUS is an abbreviation for Russia, the old country of many emigrants
FF, fortissimo, is the musical marking for very loud

explanation.surface: Noisy birds back in the homeland.
explanation.walkthrough: A ruff is a wading bird whose males grow a frilled collar in the breeding season.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruffs are sandpipers, wading birds whose males display ornamental neck feathers.

explanation.surface: An eager worker who still lost the job.
explanation.walkthrough: Fired up means enthusiastic; fired also means dismissed from work.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone keen or inflamed with enthusiasm is ardent; someone dismissed from a job has been let go.

parts.note: woollies are read as sheep and folding as penning them in a fold

explanation.surface: Experts at folding knitted jumpers.
explanation.walkthrough: A fold is a sheep pen, so folding means penning sheep, the 'woollies'.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who tend and pen flocks are experts at gathering sheep into a fold.

indicators.note: jingling coins move about in the pocket, so the letters are shaken up

explanation.surface: A child shaking the coins in a pocket.
explanation.definitionFit: A scion is a young descendant or heir of a family.

parts.note: he is the male pronoun
a tup is a ram, an uncastrated male sheep

explanation.surface: A ram worked up into a frenzy.
explanation.walkthrough: TUP is a dialect word for a ram.
explanation.definitionFit: Being agitated or worked up is to be excited.

clue.text: Musical glasses may also be blown

explanation.surface: Glassware for music that one could also blow into.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'glass harmonica' was an instrument of tuned glasses; the name is also the mouth organ, which is blown.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuned glass bowls played by touch formed an instrument of this name; a mouth organ is played by blowing.

parts.note: the remotest place, the land the ancients placed at the northern edge of the known world

explanation.surface: A remote, out-of-the-way place.
explanation.walkthrough: Ultima Thule was the classical name for the farthest northern land.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient geographers' farthest northern land became a byword for the most remote region.

parts.note: the noun that is usually paired with the adjective high to mean great resentment

explanation.surface: Someone at the peak of righteous anger.
explanation.walkthrough: One is 'in high dudgeon' when deeply offended, so this word's usual height is high.
explanation.definitionFit: This word means a feeling of offended resentment, most often met in the idiom about being high in it.

clue.text: In form, in moving how--- --and admirable! (Hamlet)

definitions.text: In form, in moving how--- --and admirable! (Hamlet)

parts.words: In form, in moving how--- --and admirable! (Hamlet)
parts.note: the missing word of Hamlet's speech praising man, meaning exact and well-made

explanation.surface: A line from Hamlet's speech on man, with one word blanked out.
explanation.walkthrough: The speech is 'What a piece of work is a man ... in form and moving how express and admirable!'; here express means precisely shaped.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's sense the word means exactly formed, well framed.
